claim: Toxoplasma gondii belongs to the phylum of Apicomplexa that groups numerous parasitic protozoans causing severe diseases in humans and animals.
source: Toxoplasma gondii belongs to the phylum of Apicomplexa that groups numerous parasitic protozoans causing severe diseases in humans and animals.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the taxonomic classification and pathogenic nature of Toxoplasma gondii and Apicomplexa.

claim: Apicomplexa are characterized by the presence of the alveoli, which consist in small flattened single-membrane sacs, underlying the plasma membrane to form the inner membrane complex (IMC) of the parasite.
source: As part of the superphylum of Alveolata, the Apicomplexa are characterized by the presence of the alveoli, which consist in small flattened single-membrane sacs, underlying the plasma membrane (PM) to form the inner membrane complex (IMC) of the parasite.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structural features of Apicomplexa.

claim: A rigid alveolin network composed of intermediate filament-like proteins is lining the cytoplasmic side of the IMC.
source: A rigid alveolin network composed of intermediate filament-like proteins is lining the cytoplasmic side of the IMC.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the alveolin network structure.

claim: The alveolin network is made of proteins sharing conserved repeat motifs called alveolins, which together with the IMC span the length of the parasite from the apical polar ring (APR) to the basal complex.
source: The alveolin network is made of proteins sharing conserved repeat motifs called alveolins, which together with the IMC span the length of the parasite from the apical polar ring (APR) to the basal complex (Mann and Beckers, 2001; Gould et al., 2008; Anderson-White et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The IMC plays an essential role in parasite motility by anchoring the actomyosin system.
source: The IMC plays an essential role in parasite motility by anchoring the actomyosin system (Frénal et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The IMC serves as structural scaffold during daughter cells formation within the mother cell, an asexual form of reproduction referred to as endodyogeny.
source: The IMC plays an essential role in parasite motility by anchoring the actomyosin system (Frénal et al., 2017) and serves as structural scaffold during daughter cells formation within the mother cell, an asexual form of reproduction referred to as endodyogeny (Francia and Striepen, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The IMC is arranged in a series of rectangular plates sutured together.
source: The IMC is arranged in a series of rectangular plates sutured together.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IMC structure.

claim: Several IMC sutures components (ISCs) have been localized to the transversal and longitudinal sutures between alveolar sacs.
source: Several IMC sutures components (ISCs) have been localized to the transversal and longitudinal sutures between alveolar sacs (Chen et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The parasite is capped by a single cone-shaped plate called the apical cap.
source: The parasite is capped by a single cone-shaped plate called the apical cap.
evidence: This is established knowledge about parasite structure.

claim: Several proteins have been reported to localize at the apical cap including the IMC sub-compartment protein 1 (ISP1) and nine apical cap proteins (called AC1 to AC9).
source: Several proteins have been reported to localize at the apical cap including the IMC sub-compartment protein 1 (ISP1) (Beck et al., 2010) and nine apical cap proteins (called AC1 to AC9) (Chen et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Centrin2 labels a peripheral ring of six annuli at the boundary of the apical plate and the rest of the alveolar plates.
source: Centrin2 labels a peripheral ring of six annuli at the boundary of the apical plate and the rest of the alveolar plates (Hu et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A set of 22 subpellicular microtubules (SPMT) spanning two third of the parasite length confers the elongated shape to the tachyzoites.
source: Beneath the alveolin network, a set of 22 subpellicular microtubules (SPMT) spanning two third of the parasite length confers the elongated shape to the tachyzoites.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structural role of SPMTs.

claim: The SPTMs originate at the APR, which serves as microtubule-organizing center (MTOC).
source: The SPTMs originate at the APR, which serves as microtubule-organizing center (MTOC).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of the APR.

claim: Ultrastructural studies have highlighted tight connections between the IMC complex and the SPMTs.
source: Ultrastructural studies have highlighted tight connections between the IMC complex and the SPMTs.
evidence: This is a general statement about findings from ultrastructural studies.

claim: Freeze-fractured studies showed double rows of inner membranous particles (IMPs) at the IMC surface arranged in spiraling longitudinal rows reminiscent of SPMT path exhibiting a repeating pattern with a 32 nm periodicity.
source: More specifically, freeze-fractured studies showed double rows of inner membranous particles (IMPs) at the IMC surface arranged in spiraling longitudinal rows reminiscent of SPMT path exhibiting a repeating pattern with a 32 nm periodicity.
evidence: This is established knowledge from freeze-fracture studies.

claim: A 32 nm periodicity was observed in the single row of IMP associated with SPMTs.
source: This 32 nm periodicity was also observed in the single row of IMP associated with SPMTs (Morrissette et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The APR and the secretory organelles, rhoptries (implicated in invasion) and micronemes (implicated in motility, invasion and egress), are common features of the apical complex conserved in all motile and invasive apicomplexans.
source: The APR and the secretory organelles, rhoptries (implicated in invasion) and micronemes (implicated in motility, invasion and egress), are common features of the apical complex conserved in all motile and invasive apicomplexans.
evidence: This is established knowledge about conserved features of apicomplexans.

claim: Members of the coccidian subgroup of the phylum, including Toxoplasma, Neospora, Besniotia, Cyclospora, Sarcocystis and Eimeria, possess an additional organelle termed the conoid.
source: Members of the coccidian subgroup of the phylum, including Toxoplasma, Neospora, Besniotia, Cyclospora, Sarcocystis and Eimeria, possess an additional organelle termed the conoid.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the taxonomic distribution of the conoid.

claim: The conoid is formed by 14 atypical comma-shape tubulin fibers composed of ∼9 protofilaments differing from classical microtubules in that they do not form a closed tubule but rather an open comma shaped structure.
source: This dynamic organelle is formed by 14 atypical comma-shape tubulin fibers composed of ∼9 protofilaments differing from classical microtubules in that they do not form a closed tubule but rather an open comma shaped structure (Hu et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The conoid is enclosed between the APR and two preconoidal rings (PCRs) at the apex of the parasite.
source: The conoid is enclosed between the APR and two preconoidal rings (PCRs) at the apex of the parasite.
evidence: This is established knowledge about conoid structure.

claim: Two short intraconoidal microtubules are present within the conoid.
source: In addition, two short intraconoidal microtubules are present within the conoid (Morrissette, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: During division, the conoid is retracted posterior to the APR whereas it protrudes through the APR in a calcium-dependent manner in motile parasites.
source: During division, the conoid is retracted posterior to the APR whereas it protrudes through the APR in a calcium-dependent manner in motile parasites (Mondragon and Frixione, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The calcium-dependent protein kinase 1 (CDPK1) is an essential regulator of microneme exocytosis.
source: The calcium-dependent protein kinase 1 (CDPK1) is an essential regulator of microneme exocytosis (Lourido et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Deletion of CDPK1 results in inhibition of conoid protrusion and a block of the apico-basal flux of F-actin, essential for parasite motility.
source: The calcium-dependent protein kinase 1 (CDPK1) is an essential regulator of microneme exocytosis (Lourido et al., 2010) and its deletion results in inhibition of conoid protrusion and a block of the apico-basal flux of F-actin, essential for parasite motility (Tosetti et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The mechanistic contribution of the conoid in motility and invasion has not been elucidated to date.
source: The mechanistic contribution of the conoid in motility and invasion has not been elucidated to date.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: During evolution, the conoid was lost in Haematozoa which include Plasmodium spp. and piroplasmidia (Theileria and Babesia).
source: During evolution, the conoid was lost in Haematozoa which include Plasmodium spp. and piroplasmidia (Theileria and Babesia).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the evolutionary loss of the conoid.

claim: The conoid is still present in deeply branching Cryptosporidium spp. and Gregarina spp.
source: In contrast, the conoid is still present in deeply branching Cryptosporidium spp. and Gregarina spp.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the presence of the conoid in certain taxa.

claim: Other more distantly related Alveolata (colpodellids, perkinsids and chromerids) possess a similar structure referred to as incomplete conoid or pseudoconoid, built from apical MTs but lacking the APR.
source: Other more distantly related Alveolata (colpodellids, perkinsids and chromerids) possess a similar structure referred to as incomplete conoid or pseudoconoid, built from apical MTs but lacking the APR, which suggests that early branching apicomplexans harbored an ancestral apical complex along with secretory organelles (Gubbels and Duraisingh, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Early branching apicomplexans harbored an ancestral apical complex along with secretory organelles.
source: Other more distantly related Alveolata (colpodellids, perkinsids and chromerids) possess a similar structure referred to as incomplete conoid or pseudoconoid, built from apical MTs but lacking the APR, which suggests that early branching apicomplexans harbored an ancestral apical complex along with secretory organelles (Gubbels and Duraisingh, 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative analysis, supported by a citation.

claim: The SAS6-like protein is localized near the base of the flagellum of Trypanosoma brucei.
source: Intriguingly, the SAS6-like protein, which is localized near the base of the flagellum of Trypanosoma brucei, is found at the preconoidal rings of T. gondii tachyzoites that do not possess a flagellum, raising questions about the origin of the conoid (de Leon et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: SAS6-like protein is found at the preconoidal rings of T. gondii tachyzoites that do not possess a flagellum.
source: Intriguingly, the SAS6-like protein, which is localized near the base of the flagellum of Trypanosoma brucei, is found at the preconoidal rings of T. gondii tachyzoites that do not possess a flagellum, raising questions about the origin of the conoid (de Leon et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: SAS6-like has been localized apically in both ookinetes and sporozoites but absent in merozoites of Plasmodium berghei.
source: SAS6-like has also been localized apically in both ookinetes and sporozoites but absent in merozoites of Plasmodium berghei, revealing that the morphology and composition of the apical complex might vary between different parasitic life stages and yet retained conserved proteins (Wall et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The morphology and composition of the apical complex might vary between different parasitic life stages and yet retained conserved proteins.
source: SAS6-like has also been localized apically in both ookinetes and sporozoites but absent in merozoites of Plasmodium berghei, revealing that the morphology and composition of the apical complex might vary between different parasitic life stages and yet retained conserved proteins (Wall et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential localization of SAS6-like, supported by a citation.

claim: More than 250 proteins were enriched in the conoid fraction by a proteomic approach.
source: More than 250 proteins were enriched in the conoid fraction by a proteomic approach (Hu et al., 2006) but only a few have been functionally investigated.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Knockdown of the APR protein RNG2 results in microneme secretion defect.
source: Knockdown of the APR protein RNG2 results in microneme secretion defect (Katris et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The conoid-associated MyoH and the likely associated calmodulin-like proteins are all required for gliding motility that powers invasion and egress.
source: while the conoid-associated MyoH and the likely associated calmodulin-like proteins are all required for gliding motility that powers invasion and egress (Graindorge et al., 2016; Long et al., 2017a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The apical complex methyltransferase (AKMT), the formin 1 (FRM1) and the glideosome-associated connector (GAC) are apical proteins conserved across the Apicomplexa that play essential roles in parasite motility, invasion and egress.
source: Additionally, the apical complex methyltransferase (AKMT) (Heaslip et al., 2011), the formin 1 (FRM1) (Tosetti et al., 2019) and the glideosome-associated connector (GAC) (Jacot et al., 2016) are apical proteins conserved across the Apicomplexa that play essential roles in parasite motility, invasion and egress (Frénal et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Loss of microtubules binding doublecortin (DCX)-domain protein results in shorter disordered conoid with subsequent defect in invasion.
source: Among the proteins involved in stability of the apical complex, loss of microtubules binding doublecortin (DCX)-domain protein results in shorter disordered conoid with subsequent defect in invasion (Nagayasu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: DCX bundles the conoidal tubulin fibers into comma-shape structures likely conferring the cone-shaped configuration of the conoid.
source: DCX was later shown to bundle the conoidal tubulin fibers into comma-shape structures likely conferring the cone-shaped configuration of the conoid (Leung et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The double knockout of kinesin A and apical polar ring protein 1 (APR1) caused a fragmentation of the APR with a conoid frequently partially detached resulting in impairment of microneme secretion.
source: Moreover, the double knockout of kinesin A and apical polar ring protein 1 (APR1) caused a fragmentation of the APR with a conoid frequently partially detached resulting in impairment of microneme secretion (Leung et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Conoid protein hub 1 (CPH1) is a conserved apicomplexan protein essential for parasite motility, invasion and egress that regulates conoid stability in extracellular parasites without impacting on microneme secretion.
source: Lastly, conoid protein hub 1 (CPH1) is a conserved apicomplexan protein essential for parasite motility, invasion and egress that regulates conoid stability in extracellular parasites without impacting on microneme secretion (Long et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The MAP kinase ERK7 localizes to the apical cap and is involved in conoid assembly without impacting on microneme secretion.
source: Similarly, a recently described protein, the MAP kinase ERK7, localizing to the apical cap is reported to be involved in conoid assembly without impacting on microneme secretion (O'Shaughnessy et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: AC10 was identified as a partner of AC9 by BioID.
source: Here, we have used ultrastructure expansion microscopy (U-ExM) to precisely localize AC9 and its partner AC10, identified by BioID, to the alveolin network but exclusively in the apical cap region in-between the SPMTs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: AC9 and AC10 localize to the alveolin network but exclusively in the apical cap region in-between the SPMTs.
source: Here, we have used ultrastructure expansion microscopy (U-ExM) to precisely localize AC9 and its partner AC10, identified by BioID, to the alveolin network but exclusively in the apical cap region in-between the SPMTs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on U-ExM data.

claim: Conditional depletion of AC9 and AC10 established that the two proteins are essential for parasite motility invasion and egress, while parasite replication is not affected.
source: Conditional depletion of AC9 and AC10 established that the two proteins are essential for parasite motility invasion and egress, while parasite replication is not affected.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data from conditional depletion experiments.

claim: AC9 or AC10 depleted mature parasites are conoidless, devoid of APR and their SPMTs are disorganized.
source: U-ExM and electron microscopy revealed striking morphological defects. AC9 or AC10 depleted mature parasites are conoidless, devoid of APR and their SPMTs are disorganized.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on U-ExM and electron microscopy data.

claim: The arrangement of AC9 and AC10 suggests that both proteins act as a glue between SPMTs, a prerequisite to maintain the overall architecture of the key components of the apical complex when the parasite matures.
source: The arrangement of AC9 and AC10 suggests that both proteins act as a glue between SPMTs, a prerequisite to maintain the overall architecture of the key components of the apical complex when the parasite matures.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization and depletion phenotypes observed in the study.

claim: T. gondii AC9 is an hypothetical protein exhibiting no informative protein domain to unravel its function but a strong negative fitness score indicative of essentiality.
source: T. gondii AC9 is an hypothetical protein exhibiting no informative protein domain to unravel its function but a strong negative fitness score indicative of essentiality (Sidik et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: AC9 colocalizes with ISP1 at the most apical plate of the IMC termed apical cap, delimited by the peripheral annuli stained by centrin2.
source: As previously reported (Chen et al., 2017), AC9 colocalizes with ISP1 at the most apical plate of the IMC termed apical cap, delimited by the peripheral annuli stained by centrin2 (Cen2).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and confirmed by the current study's observations.

claim: AC9 appears very early during endodyogeny before the emergence of the daughter parasite scaffold stained with IMC1 antibodies.
source: AC9 appears very early during endodyogeny before the emergence of the daughter parasite scaffold stained with IMC1 antibodies (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: AC9 surrounds the APR marked by RNG2-Ty.
source: Further colocalization with other Ty-tagged proteins at their endogenous loci, revealed that AC9 surrounds the APR marked by RNG2-Ty (Katris et al., 2014) and the conoid localized with CPH1-Ty (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: AC9 surrounds the conoid localized with CPH1-Ty.
source: Further colocalization with other Ty-tagged proteins at their endogenous loci, revealed that AC9 surrounds the APR marked by RNG2-Ty (Katris et al., 2014) and the conoid localized with CPH1-Ty (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: GAP70-mycGFP localized slightly more apically compared to AC9, which remains confined to the apical plate of the IMC.
source: GAP70-mycGFP localized slightly more apically compared to AC9, which remains confined to the apical plate of the IMC (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: AC9 is completely resistant to extraction with the non-ionic detergent Triton X-100 but is solubilized in sodium carbonate at pH 11.
source: Next, fractionation assay revealed that AC9 is completely resistant to extraction with the non-ionic detergent Triton X-100 but is solubilized in sodium carbonate at pH 11.
evidence: This claim is supported by fractionation assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: AC9 is an alveolin network resident protein associated to other alveolins proteins or a peripheral IMC protein.
source: This suggests that AC9 is an alveolin network resident protein associated to other alveolins proteins or a peripheral IMC protein (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the fractionation assay results.

claim: AC9-mAID-HA migrated on SDS-PAGE at around 70 kDa, slightly higher than the predicted size (60 kDa).
source: Noteworthy, AC9-mAID-HA migrated on SDS-PAGE at around 70 kDa, slightly higher than the predicted size (60 kDa).
evidence: This is an observation from SDS-PAGE analysis.

claim: In absence of biotin, apicoplast endogenously biotinylated proteins were observed while addition of biotin for 24 hr resulted in accumulation of biotinylated proteins in the apical cap, proving that the enzyme is active at the right position.
source: To assess whether AC9-mycBirA was able to biotinylate proximal proteins, we performed IFA with fluorophore-conjugated streptavidin. In absence of biotin, apicoplast endogenously biotinylated proteins were observed while addition of biotin for 24 hr resulted in accumulation of biotinylated proteins in the apical cap, proving that the enzyme is active at the right position (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by IFA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Deoxycholate extracted parasites showed a robust streptavidin staining around the apical cortical microtubules just beneath the conoid indicating biotinylation of components of the parasite cytoskeleton.
source: Of relevance, deoxycholate extracted parasites showed a robust streptavidin staining around the apical cortical microtubules just beneath the conoid indicating biotinylation of components of the parasite cytoskeleton (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: TGGT1_292950 was the clear top hit in the mass spectrometry analysis of AC9-BirA biotinylated proteins.
source: The clear top hit was a hypothetical protein (TGGT1_292950) followed by two apical cap proteins (AC2 and AC8) and IMC/cytoskeletal proteins (Supplementary file 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: TGGT1_292950 exhibited a very similar cyclic mRNA expression pattern compared to AC9.
source: TGGT1_292950 exhibited a very similar cyclic mRNA expression pattern compared to AC9 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by expression data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Upon C-terminal Ty-epitope tagging, the product of the gene colocalized with AC9 in mature parasites and daughter cells and hence was named AC10.
source: Upon C-terminal Ty-epitope tagging, the product of the gene colocalized with AC9 in mature parasites and daughter cells and hence was named AC10 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: AC10 was partially solubilized by sodium carbonate and completely insoluble in Triton X-100, indicating its alveolin network association.
source: Like AC9, AC10 was showed to be partially solubilized by sodium carbonate and completely insoluble in Triton X-100 using the AC10-mAID-HA strain, indicating its alveolin network association (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by fractionation assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: AC9 and AC10 are recruited very early to the daughter cytoskeleton, prior to ISP1 incorporation.
source: Colocalization experiments revealed that AC9 and AC10 are recruited very early to the daughter cytoskeleton, prior to ISP1 incorporation (Figure 2A–B)
evidence: This claim is supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: AC2 and AC8 are recruited later than AC9 and AC10 during daughter cell formation.
source: in contrast, AC2 and AC8 are recruited later (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B), as schematized in Figure 2C.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Deletion of AC9 had no impact on the localization of AC2, AC8, AC10 and ISP1.
source: Deletion of AC9 had no impact on the localization of AC2, AC8, AC10 and ISP1 (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by IFA data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Epitope-tagged AC9 in AC10-mAID-HA disappeared upon AC10 depletion both by western blot and indirect immunofluorescence assay.
source: Conversely, epitope-tagged AC9 in AC10-mAID-HA disappeared upon AC10 depletion both by western blot (WB) and indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA) (Figure 2E–F) providing additional compelling evidence that the two proteins form a complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by WB and IFA data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: AC9 and AC10 form a complex.
source: Conversely, epitope-tagged AC9 in AC10-mAID-HA disappeared upon AC10 depletion both by western blot (WB) and indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA) (Figure 2E–F) providing additional compelling evidence that the two proteins form a complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the co-dependence of AC9 and AC10 stability.

claim: A short treatment with IAA was sufficient to cause destabilization of AC9.
source: Even a short treatment with IAA was sufficient to cause destabilization of AC9 (Figure 2G) without impacting on AC2, AC8 and ISP1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: AC9 and AC10 signals are organized in rows with a regular periodicity as revealed by STED microscopy.
source: Super-resolution imaging with a stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscope revealed that AC9 and AC10 signals are not homogeneous at the apical cap but rather organized in rows with a regular periodicity (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: IMC1 staining is organized in regular rows reminiscent of the SPMTs arrangement and the intramembranous particle lattice observed by electron microscopy.
source: Remarkably, IMC1 staining is also organized in regular rows reminiscent of the SPMTs arrangement and the intramembranous particle lattice observed by electron microscopy (EM) (Morrissette et al., 1997).
evidence: This is an observation from the current study with reference to previous EM studies.

claim: Microtubules are interspaced by two rows of IMC1.
source: Further colocalization of IMC1 with tubulin showed that microtubules are interspaced by two rows of IMC1, a pattern not reported before (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GAP45 staining is more homogeneous along the parasite pellicle on the PM side of the IMC.
source: In contrast, GAP45 staining is more homogeneous along the parasite pellicle on the PM side of the IMC.
evidence: This is an observation from the current study.

claim: AC9 is confined to the SPMTs side of the IMC and follows a periodic arrangement like SPMTs and alveolins.
source: Colocalization with GAP45 and IMC sub-compartment protein 1 (ISP1) (Beck et al., 2010) confirmed that AC9 is confined to the SPMTs side of the IMC and follows a periodic arrangement like SPMTs and alveolins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The expansion rate of U-ExM was approaching 4x.
source: The shape and ultrastructure of the parasite were well preserved while the expansion rate was approaching 4x and the SPMTs showed noticeably a high level of poly-glutamylation all along their length, except at their most distal part (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a measurement from the U-ExM experiments.

claim: The SPMTs showed a high level of poly-glutamylation all along their length, except at their most distal part.
source: The shape and ultrastructure of the parasite were well preserved while the expansion rate was approaching 4x and the SPMTs showed noticeably a high level of poly-glutamylation all along their length, except at their most distal part (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The conoid fibers seem to be devoid of poly-glutamylation.
source: Interestingly the conoid fibers seem to be devoid of poly-glutamylation.
evidence: This is an observation from the U-ExM experiments.

claim: AC9 and AC10 were clearly colocalizing as a regular pattern between each SPMTs just below the conoid and the APR.
source: Of relevance, AC9 and AC10 were clearly colocalizing as a regular pattern between each SPMTs just below the conoid and the APR (Figure 3C–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data shown in Figure 3C-E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: AC9 did not interact directly with porcine microtubules in an in vitro binding assay.
source: AC9 did not interact directly with these heterologous MTs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: AC2 is localized on the SPMTs up to the APR.
source: Analysis of the other ACs biotinylated proteins by AC9 revealed that AC2 is localized on the SPMTs up to the APR in contrast to AC8, which is present between the SPMTs and does not reach the APR (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: AC8 is present between the SPMTs and does not reach the APR.
source: Analysis of the other ACs biotinylated proteins by AC9 revealed that AC2 is localized on the SPMTs up to the APR in contrast to AC8, which is present between the SPMTs and does not reach the APR (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: AC9 and AC10 surround the APR stained by RNG2 without being in direct contact with it.
source: STED microscopy confirmed that AC9 and AC10 are surrounding the APR stained by RNG2 without being in direct contact with it (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: RNG2 adopted a regular pattern at the APR both by STED and U-ExM, suggesting that the APR is composed of discrete subunits.
source: Of interest, RNG2 adopted a regular pattern at the APR both by STED and U-ExM, suggesting that the APR is composed of discrete subunits possibly including microtubule plus-end tracking proteins that ensure the apical docking of the SPMTs and their regular interspacing (Figure 3H–I).
evidence: This is an inference based on the regular pattern of RNG2 observed by STED and U-ExM.

claim: AC9 and AC10 are tightly downregulated upon addition of auxin.
source: Upon addition of auxin, AC9 and AC10 are tightly downregulated as shown by IFA (Figure 4A and Figure 4D) and WB (Figure 4B and Figure 4E)
evidence: This claim is supported by IFA and WB data shown in Figure 4A, 4B, 4D, and 4E.

claim: Depletion of both AC9 and AC10 resulted in no lysis plaques in the monolayer of human foreskin fibroblasts after 7 days.
source: Depletion of both proteins resulted in no lysis plaques in the monolayer of human foreskin fibroblasts (HFF) after 7 days (Figure 4C and Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by plaque assay data shown in Figure 4C and 4F.

claim: Depletion of AC9 and AC10 caused a severe defect in invasion.
source: Further phenotyping showed that depletion of AC9 and AC10 caused a severe defect in invasion (Figure 4G)
evidence: This claim is supported by invasion assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Depletion of AC9 and AC10 caused a severe defect in egress.
source: Further phenotyping showed that depletion of AC9 and AC10 caused a severe defect in invasion (Figure 4G) and egress (Figure 4H)
evidence: This claim is supported by egress assay data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Depletion of AC9 and AC10 did not impact on parasite intracellular growth and replication.
source: Further phenotyping showed that depletion of AC9 and AC10 caused a severe defect in invasion (Figure 4G) and egress (Figure 4H) without impacting on parasite intracellular growth and replication (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by intracellular growth assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Depletion of AC9 and AC10 caused a severe block in induced microneme secretion upon stimulation by BIPPO and ethanol.
source: This phenotype is at least in part explained by the severe block in induced microneme secretion observed upon stimulation by two known triggers of microneme exocytosis, BIPPO (a phosphodiesterase inhibitor) (Howard et al., 2015) and ethanol (Carruthers et al., 1999; Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by microneme secretion assay data shown in Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In the absence of AC9 or AC10, MyoH and RNG2 were no longer detectable at the apical complex.
source: In the absence of AC9 or AC10, numerous proteins crucially implicated in motility, invasion and conoid stability were no longer detectable at the apical complex and notably the conoid-associated motor MyoH (Graindorge et al., 2016) and the apical polar ring resident protein RNG2 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by IFA data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the absence of AC9 or AC10, AKMT, CPH1, and FRM1 were no longer detectable at the apical complex.
source: Among other apical proteins lost, we found the apical methyltransferase (AKMT) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; Heaslip et al., 2011), the conoid ankyrin-repeat containing protein hub 1 (CPH1) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and the apical actin nucleator FRM1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C; Tosetti et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by IFA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: ICMAP1 was still detectable but mispositioned in the absence of AC9 or AC10.
source: Conversely, ICMAP1, a MTs binding protein localizing to the intraconoidal microtubules (Heaslip et al., 2009) was still detectable but mispositioned (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by IFA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: All the proteins lost in the conoid of the mature parasite were still present in the forming daughter cells.
source: Remarkably, all the proteins lost in the conoid of the mature parasite (mother) were still present in the forming daughter cells suggesting that these markers were lost during the last step of daughter cell formation.
evidence: This is an observation from IFA experiments.

claim: FIB-SEM confirmed that loss of AC9 impacted the conoid and APR exclusively in the mother cell.
source: Focus Ion Beam Scanning Electron Microscopy (FIB-SEM) on intracellular parasites compellingly revealed that the conoid is absent in mature parasites while it is still visible in daughter cells, thus explaining the loss of apical markers only after completion of parasite division (Figure 5C and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by FIB-SEM data shown in Figure 5C and Video 1.

claim: The accumulation of micronemes at the very tip of the parasites was absent in AC9 depleted parasites.
source: The accumulation of micronemes at the very tip of the parasites was absent in AC9 depleted parasites and in some cases gave the impression that the organelles were in the vacuolar space (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by IFA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Some AC9 depleted parasites displayed an apical dilatation of the PM into the PV space by EM.
source: Consistent with the sporadic vacuolar staining observed with anti-MIC2 antibodies, some parasites displayed an apical dilatation of the PM into the PV space by EM (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Rhoptries were still attached to parasite apex but less bundled compared to untreated parasites in AC9 depleted parasites.
source: Moreover, rhoptries were still attached to parasite apex but less bundled compared to untreated parasites (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: 2 hr of incubation in presence of IAA were sufficient to degrade AC9 by WB in intracellular parasites.
source: Importantly, 2 hr of incubation in presence of IAA were sufficient to degrade AC9 by WB in intracellular parasites (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by WB data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Non-dividing extracellular parasites treated overnight with IAA showed no loss of apical markers as illustrated by staining of MyoH.
source: Non-dividing extracellular parasites treated overnight with IAA showed no loss of apical markers as illustrated by staining of MyoH (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by IFA data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Intracellular parasites treated with IAA showed that MyoH disappeared from the conoid only in parasites that had completed at least one cycle of division, that is after at least 4 hr of IAA treatment.
source: In contrast, intracellular parasites treated with IAA at different time points, showed that MyoH disappeared from the conoid only in parasites that had completed at least one cycle of division, that is after at least 4 hr of IAA treatment (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by IFA data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Extracellular parasites treated with IAA were not affected in microneme secretion.
source: Concordantly, extracellular parasites treated with IAA were not affected in microneme secretion (Figure 6C)
evidence: This claim is supported by microneme secretion assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Treatment of intracellular parasites with IAA led to a gradual increase in microneme secretion defects over time.
source: whereas treatment on intracellular parasites led to a gradual increase in microneme secretion defects over time (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by microneme secretion assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In the absence of AC9 or AC10, APR1 and KinA are lost in mature parasites, but present in daughter cells.
source: Next, we assessed the fate of APR markers such as kinesinA (KinA) and APR1, which are incorporated very early (Leung et al., 2017) and RNG1 a late marker of division (Tran et al., 2010). In the absence of AC9 or AC10, APR1 and KinA are lost in mature parasites, but present in daughter cells, respectively (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by IFA data shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: RNG1 is incorporated very late in daughter cells.
source: We confirmed the late incorporation of RNG1 in daughter cells (Figure 6F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by IFA data shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: In presence of IAA, RNG1 failed to localize at the APR when daughter cells were emerging from the mother cell, resulting in disorganized dots.
source: In presence of IAA, RNG1 failed to localize at the APR when daughter cells were emerging from the mother cell, resulting in disorganized dots (Figure 6F–G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by IFA data shown in Figure 6F-G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: The conoid is not lost in a synchronous manner, at least during the first 2 division cycles.
source: Interestingly, IFA performed on intracellular parasites fixed earlier post-invasion revealed that the conoid is not lost in a synchronous manner, at least during the first 2 division cycles (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by IFA data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: In AC9 and AC10 depleted parasites, the SPMTs were disconnected.
source: Deoxycholate extraction revealed that in the AC9 and AC10 depleted parasites, the SPMTs were disconnected (Figure 7A–B)
evidence: This claim is supported by deoxycholate extraction and microscopy data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: Electron microscopy revealed that the mature parasite mutants are conoidless.
source: Electron microscopy revealed that the mature parasite mutants are conoidless, while U-ExM highlighted the disorganization of the SPMTs which likely results in the catastrophic loss of APR and conoid.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from electron microscopy experiments.

claim: U-ExM highlighted the disorganization of the SPMTs in AC9 and AC10 depleted parasites.
source: Electron microscopy revealed that the mature parasite mutants are conoidless, while U-ExM highlighted the disorganization of the SPMTs which likely results in the catastrophic loss of APR and conoid.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from U-ExM experiments.

claim: The disorganization of the SPMTs likely results in the catastrophic loss of APR and conoid.
source: Electron microscopy revealed that the mature parasite mutants are conoidless, while U-ExM highlighted the disorganization of the SPMTs which likely results in the catastrophic loss of APR and conoid.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed disorganization of SPMTs and loss of APR and conoid.

claim: U-ExM confirmed that parasites depleted of AC9 and AC10 presented an enlarged apical opening.
source: When applying U-ExM in AC9 and AC10 depleted parasites, loss of APR and conoid were confirmed and the apex appeared enlarged.
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data.

claim: SPMTs appeared significantly disorganized at the apical pole of mature parasites depleted of AC9 and AC10.
source: Remarkably, SPMTs appeared significantly disorganized at the apical pole of mature parasites (Figure 7C–F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data shown in Figure 7C-F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The depletion of AC9 resulted in the loss of the preconoidal rings while the peripheral annuli were not affected.
source: Of relevance, the depletion of AC9 resulted in the loss of the preconoidal rings while the peripheral annuli were not affected, when visualized by Centrin2 labeling (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: AC9 and AC10 are conserved uniquely in the cyst forming coccidian subgroup of Apicomplexa that includes T. gondii, Neospora caninum, Besnoitia besnoiti and Cystoisospora suis.
source: Of note, AC9 and AC10 are conserved uniquely in the cyst forming coccidian subgroup of Apicomplexa that includes T. gondii, Neospora caninum, Besnoitia besnoiti and Cystoisospora suis.
evidence: This is an observation from comparative genomics analysis.

claim: AC9 and AC10 are absent in Eimeria spp., piroplasmida, haemosporidia and cryptosporidia.
source: Both proteins are absent in Eimeria spp., piroplasmida, haemosporidia and cryptosporidia, while other ACs appear to be conserved in other lineages including distantly related gregarines and chromerids.
evidence: This is an observation from comparative genomics analysis.

claim: The cascade of events leading to the loss of the conoid and APR involves parasite division.
source: The cascade of events leading to the loss of the conoid and APR involves parasite division.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of conoid and APR loss observed in the experiments.

claim: The conoid and APR are present in growing daughter cells and are only lost at the final stage of endodyogeny, when the daughter cells emerge and their cytoskeleton confers shape and rigidity to the parasite.
source: Strikingly, the conoid and APR are present in growing daughter cells and are only lost at the final stage of endodyogeny, when the daughter cells emerge and their cytoskeleton confers shape and rigidity to the parasite.
evidence: This is a summary of observations from time-course experiments.

claim: The detached conoid appears to be very rapidly degraded.
source: The detached conoid appears to be very rapidly degraded because we fail to detect it inside mature parasites even when scrutinizing with FIB-SEM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the failure to detect the conoid in mature parasites by FIB-SEM.

claim: In deoxycholate extracted AC9 and AC10 depleted parasites, the SPMTs are formed properly but are not joint together by the APR, which is absent in these mutants.
source: In deoxycholate extracted AC9 and AC10 depleted parasites, the SPMTs are formed properly but are not joint together by the APR, which is absent in these mutants.
evidence: This is an observation from deoxycholate extraction experiments.

claim: The strategic position of AC9 and AC10 intercalated between SPTMs suggested a possible implication in maintaining the correct interspacing between the SPMTs.
source: The strategic position of AC9 and AC10 intercalated between SPTMs suggested a possible implication in maintaining the correct interspacing between the SPMTs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization of AC9 and AC10.

claim: The dramatic consequences of AC9 and AC10 depletion on SPTMs, APR and conoid occur very late during parasite division.
source: The dramatic consequences of AC9 and AC10 depletion on SPTMs, APR and conoid occur very late during parasite division (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a summary of observations from time-course experiments.

claim: At the time when the daughter cells emerge from the mother cell, the tension imposed on the SPMTs could plausibly lead to their disorganization and consequently to the loss of APR and conoid.
source: At the time when the daughter cells emerge from the mother cell, the tension imposed on the SPMTs could plausibly lead to their disorganization and consequently to the loss of APR and conoid and hence explains why the phenotypes of AC9 and AC10 depletion only appear at the end of the division process.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the timing of the phenotype.

claim: The loss of the conoid is presumably a consequence of the loss of the APR, which could result from the disorganization of the SPMTs at the apical pole of the parasite.
source: Taken together, these findings lead us to postulate that the loss of the conoid is presumably a consequence of the loss of the APR, which could result from the disorganization of the SPMTs at the apical pole of the parasite.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: The AC9/AC10 complex would act as a glue in between SPMTs and establish a functional link between the alveolin network and the SPMTs.
source: In such a model, the AC9/AC10 complex would act as a glue in between SPMTs and establish a functional link between the alveolin network and the SPMTs.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings.
